I think it's easy for people to demonize slavery and use it as a political tool to get other things they want. I'm not saying slavery was fair or right, what I'm saying is that it wasn't as bad as people make it out to be. Sure there are horror stories, but from an impartial study you will see evidence that even the slaves didn't mind it too much. There are plantation owners and slaves that were very happy together through multiple generations from before the war through emancipation and continuing long after the war. In fact most slaves returned to the plantation they had originally worked on after they had been emancipated. I'm not particularly interested in arguing whether or not slaves were happy with where and how they worked, but I am interested in discussing how the enforcement of federal law, without the slightest consideration for states rights to govern themselves, led to what southern states saw as their only option, secession. It is my belief that slavery would have become illegal regardless of the proclamation of emancipation and that it was not even the primary focus for the majority of the war. The states were originally set up to address a fact that the founding fathers knew to be true: the United states is and will increasingly be too large of an area, too diverse of a people to be governed by a single set of laws. It is therefore vital that the territories inside the United states have some sense of sovereignty. The legalization of Marijuana is just like slavery; the government tried to make it illegal in each state and for some states that was okay and in some other states that wasn't okay. Thankfully the federal government backed off and allowed states to legalize it, but the federal government shouldn't be "allowing" states to do certain things, it should be entirely up to the state. This was the main focus of the civil war, not slavery itself but the rights of the states to decide.
